input:
In this example we consider a single-stage compressor that raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar, the air entering the machine at an inlet temperature of 293 K, and we ask what discharge temperature the standard isentropic analysis predicts. Carrying out that analysis gives a discharge temperature of 450 K.

The analysis rests on the customary idealisations. The compression is treated as though it were both reversible and adiabatic, and air is treated as an ideal gas whose heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 remains constant throughout the process. On the basis of those assumptions, the discharge temperature turns out to depend only on the inlet temperature and on the pressure ratio between discharge and inlet, and practical details such as the dimensions of the machine, the speed at which it runs, and the design of its valves have no influence on the result, since the isentropic end state is fixed by the two pressures alone.

One qualification must, however, be kept firmly in mind: the isentropic estimate makes no allowance at all for mechanical losses. In the installed machine, friction in the bearings and seals and the irreversibilities associated with flow through the valves convert a part of the shaft work into additional heat, and consequently the discharge temperature actually measured on the installed machine will be higher than the estimated value. The estimate is therefore most properly used as a baseline figure, for preliminary sizing of the discharge cooler, for checking against temperature limits imposed by seals or lubricants, and as a reference against which measured temperatures can be compared when the condition of the machine is being assessed.
target:
A single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar, with an inlet temperature of 293 K. The discharge temperature on the isentropic estimate is 450 K.

The estimate treats the compression as reversible and adiabatic, and air as an ideal gas with a constant heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 over the temperature range. On those assumptions, the discharge temperature is fixed by the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio; the size of the machine, its speed, and the design of its valves do not enter the calculation, because an isentropic end state between two pressures does not depend on the path the machine takes between them.

The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. Friction in the bearings and seals, and the irreversibility of the flow through the valves, convert part of the shaft work into heat in the gas, so the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher than the estimate. The estimated temperature is a baseline: it serves a first sizing of the discharge cooler, a check against temperature limits set by seals or lubricant, and a reference for the measured temperature when the condition of the machine is judged. Where a decision turns on the temperature the machine actually reaches, the measured discharge temperature displaces the estimate. A higher pressure ratio at the same inlet temperature gives a higher discharge temperature; the estimate moves with the duty in that direction, by the relation the assumptions fix.
